Removing build.rs will remove go build from cargo lifecycle. The file is still incomplete though, I have to add few functionalities and assert checks for it. Build.rs is a common practice in Rust to build external language dependencies like cc, cxx, swift, etc.
Regarding cargo zig build should be able to build rn, because the dependencies are under compat. But worth to keep an eye on it

Also is counter productive run go build and cargo build for every change on opencode. Are you asking it because of concerns for goreleaser? We can also add a cargo env parameter that allow receive the binary from a specific source. Many build.rs does that

In this case we might just use if cases instead of a switch and order the priority as we want

> I see in the video above that you can scroll down and there is empty space why is that ? @kujtimiihoxha The diffview accepts an `yOffset` option to skip (scroll) a given number of lines from the top. We're simply mimicing modern code editors that allow you to scroll beyond the end of the file. Remember that diffview will be a generic standard component, and that may be nice in some scenarios. Andrey this is absolutely incredible. I'd make two changes:

1. I'd add bind <kbd>shift+hjkl</kbd> to the navigation bindings
2. Currently you can scroll horizontally and vertically endlessly. I'd change it so that scrolling stops when there's no more content to show, so you essentially can't scroll endlessly.

I'm on the fence about scrolling beyond the bounds, but let's keep it for now and get a feel for it.

no strong opinions either way, but, we should probably have a "standard" for that internally.

## Image Pasting in Claude Code vs Cursor

### Claude Code
Claude Code supports image pasting through multiple methods:
1. **Drag and drop** - Drop an image file into the Claude Code window
2. **Clipboard paste** - Copy an image and paste it using **Ctrl+V** (not Cmd+V on Mac)
3. **File path reference** - Provide a path like `/path/to/image.png`

The documentation specifically mentions using **Ctrl+V** for pasting images from clipboard.

### Cursor IDE
Cursor also supports image pasting but with some limitations:
- **Chat area**: Full Ctrl+V clipboard support for images
- **Edit box**: Limited support - requires drag & drop or saving image first, then referencing it with @ symbol
- Users can take screenshots and paste directly into chat for visual communication

### The Issue
It seems like there might be a keybinding conflict where Ctrl+V is opening nvim instead of pasting the image. This could be:
1. A terminal/shell configuration issue (iTerm2/zsh keybindings)
2. A conflict with system keybindings
3. A potential issue with how crush handles the Ctrl+V shortcut

### Suggested Investigation
- Check if this happens in other terminals besides iTerm2
- Test with different shell configurations
- Verify if crush is properly handling the Ctrl+V keybinding for image paste vs text paste

* Add a new provider `type`, say `openai-responses`, that converts the whole provider to using the new API.
* Add a model flag, so this can be switched on just for certain models, such as the new models that require it.

As @hutchisr pointed out, this is going to mean entering a game of cat-and-mouse with Anthropic. It's not a matter of just implementing OAuth support; you have to keep up with Anthropic's defensive practices, which now include checking each API request used with a subscription token to try detect whether the request is coming from Claude Code - not just through "spoofable" things like headers, but by the _content that gets sent to the model_.

There are workarounds at the moment (which OpenCode is rightly hesitant to detail - https://github.com/sst/opencode/issues/417#issuecomment-3010089994) but in the long run Anthropic will almost certainly win this battle if they want to. To the fullest extent of their existing practices, you can literally only use these subscription tokens if your request includes the full Claude Code system prompt and toolset, which is proprietary, and even aside from it being proprietary, it influences model behavior which will harm anyone's (Crush, OpenCode, etc.) ability to differentiate _their_ coding agent from Claude Code.

To be clear, I want this too, just don't blame Crush for not doing this yet, as if it's easy or just an oversight. :) The pressure should really be on Anthropic imo.

According to the [GitHub Copilot Extension Developer Policy](https://docs.github.com/en/site-policy/github-terms/github-copilot-extension-developer-policy#2-developing-your-extension), section 2:

> ... Extensions and developers must not:
> - Degrade or compromise security
> - Bypass or circumvent protocols and access controls
> - **Use unpublished APIs**

(emphasis mine)

GitHub doesn't publish an official Copilot API, and instead exposes its functionality through first party extensions and services. All unofficial wrappers access this unpublished API, which is in direct violation of this policy.

Edit: and as I mentioned above, it is possible to use copilot with crush through the use of [`copilot-api`](https://github.com/ericc-ch/copilot-api) which wraps these unpublished APIs into an OpenAI compatible server. @anuramat was kind enough to provide the crush config required to do that.

For anyone else investigating this: The problem is that the entire candidate list is generated pre-hoc (including all recursive files!), doing this in e.g. a large monorepo just blows up everything (and caching will also not help in this case, as the original operation will already block for a long time or never even complete).

A "proper" fix is actually quite difficult, for example: The completion logic could be refactored to be able to lazily generate the candidate list (e.g. read from the filesystem with a non-strict iterator, cache all seen files during the completion, and lazily load more so that there's always ~10 candidates available). Doing this correctly is not easy.

A much simpler way would be to not do fuzzy matching on the full path, and complete individual path segments instead. But this is a functionality change ...

If crush doesn't show Qwen3 Coder (free) even after editing crush.json, the issue is likely that Crush overwrites its own providers.json at runtime.

Root Cause: Crush replaces your config with its internal default unless you patch the installed package's providers.json.

Fix Summary:

1, Locate Crush install dir:


C:\Users\(put your username here)\AppData\Roaming\npm\node_modules\@charmland\crush
In that folder, edit or replace providers.json to include:


{
  "id": "qwen/qwen3-coder:free",
  "name": "Qwen: Qwen3 Coder (free)",
  "cost_per_1m_in": 0,
  "cost_per_1m_out": 0,
  "context_window": 262144,
  "default_max_tokens": 32768,
  ...
}

2, And update the provider's default_small_model_id to:


"default_small_model_id": "qwen/qwen3-coder:free"

3, Prevent future overwrites with PowerShell:

attrib +R "C:\Users\(put your username here)\AppData\Roaming\npm\node_modules\@charmland\crush\providers.json"
attrib +R "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\crush\providers.json"
Restart Crush — the model should now persist across sessions.

Pro tip: Backup the folder first in case you need to restore defaults.

This is working for me, thank you!   Noting current STDIO behavior in case other people start looking:

 * If one starts a STDIO MCP server, the process will stay alive after the tool call and show the Green Dot.
 * If that MCP server process is killed, the Crush MCP Green Dot will remain.  Crush doesn't know the transport state unless it tries to read/write periodically ([MCP ping](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-03-26/basic/utilities/ping)).
 * If the STDIO MCP Server is dead, a new process is created and everything works fine (assuming it starts properly). I don't think there is logging of its demise.

Note, this required 4 internal tools to be added, not 2, to work correctly. Crush has a bad habit of trying to incorrectly guess the names of the lsp and mcp servers that are running, and had no introspection into their names before. So, in addition to the restart tools (1 mcp, 1 lsp) I added a tool for listing the mcps and one for listing the lsps.

Right now, permissions for these tools are manually granted. If we want, we can enable the list permission to be granted automatically, since it's non-destructive. 

Same goes for restarting the LSPs/MCPs, but it's probably best to request permissions for that, since it kills running processes and restarts them.

@jamestrew, Thanks for the feedback! For some context: in the **Discord discussions** with the maintainers and contributors (Christian, Kujtim, Manu, JD, and others), it was agreed that `@` should remain **reserved for a future feature**, so it’s not suitable to use it right now for file references.

That’s why the consolidated proposal is:

* `/` → quick commands (e.g., `/exit`, `/mcp`)
* `#` → references to files already indexed in the project (with line support, e.g., `#src/main.py:42`)
* `~` → paths relative to the project root (e.g., `~docs/guide.md`)
* `>` → direct shell/script execution (e.g., `>npm run dev`)
* `f:` → quick file search by name (e.g., `f:config.json`)

### Key points discussed on Discord:

* **Christian** and **Kujtim**: gave positive feedback and supported the proposal, even pinning the message as reference.
* **JD**: emphasized that using `@` for files creates conflicts in tools like Claude Code, slowing things down in large projects.
* **Manu**: suggested using `!` for shell commands (as in Vim/Neovim and Jupyter). We debated pros and cons, and agreed that `>` avoids conflicts (with Bash history, logical operators, Git, etc.) and ensures predictability across all environments.
* **Kujtim**: asked about the difference between `#` and `~`. We aligned that `#` always refers to a file already indexed in the project context (with full integration), while `~` is just a literal path relative to the root, including docs and assets outside the workspace.

This mapping was designed to **reduce the learning curve**, **avoid collisions**, and create a clear and consistent grammar in Crush—benefiting both CLI and IDE users.

I've opened https://github.com/charmbracelet/crush/pull/914, which takes a step in this direction.

It doesn't let you add your own subagents. It turns out though that Crush already has one hardcoded subagent - the task subagent. The top-level "coder" agent can defer open ended "find how this works" or "find where this is implemented" style tasks to the "task" agent.

My main goal with #914 was to let you pick which model which agent uses. As part of that though I've updated the sidebar and splash screen to show what agents exist and what models they're using.

I've also added an `agents` config block that currently just lets you configure the model for the two built in agents. I could imagine a future PR extending the agents block to allow you to:

* Define new agents
* Specify what model they should use
* Specify what tools they can use

# Comment for GitHub Issues #472 and #727

## Investigation Findings: Root Causes of Compaction Hanging

I've done a deep dive into the codebase and found several critical issues causing the compaction hanging behavior:

### 🐛 Critical Bug Found

There's a bug in `/internal/llm/agent/agent.go` line 814 where error handling uses an undefined variable:

```go
// Current (BROKEN):
Error: fmt.Errorf("failed to summarize: %w", err)  // 'err' is undefined!

// Should be:
Error: fmt.Errorf("failed to summarize: %w", r.Error)
```

**This bug prevents ANY error messages from being shown during compaction failures**, which explains why you're seeing "nothing happens" - errors are occurring but not being displayed!

### ⏱️ No Timeouts

The compaction process has no timeout configured. It uses `context.WithCancel()` instead of `context.WithTimeout()`, meaning it can run forever if the provider doesn't respond or is very slow.

### 📊 No Progress Feedback

The UI only shows generic messages like "Compacting Session..." without any details about:
- Token count being processed
- Time elapsed
- Retry attempts
- Provider status

### For OpenRouter users (#472)

OpenRouter errors (rate limits, provider issues) are being swallowed by the bug above. The providers might be failing but you'll never see the error.

### For Ollama users (#727)

Local models like Qwen3 0.6b can be VERY slow for summarization tasks, especially with limited context (2048 tokens). Without timeout or progress feedback, it appears frozen even if it's actually processing.

## Workarounds (until fixed)

1. **Check logs**: Run crush with `--debug` flag and check `~/.local/share/crush/logs/crush.log` for actual errors
2. **Smaller sessions**: Try to compact before reaching high context usage
3. **Faster models**: If using Ollama, try a faster/larger model for summarization if possible

## Proposed Fix

I've documented the complete fix in a separate issue, but the immediate changes needed are:
1. Fix the error variable bug (one-line change)
2. Add a 5-minute timeout
3. Show progress updates every few seconds

- We did not use the main loop context so when you cancel the request or the main agent is done the loop was continuing.

Not sure when they'll work on that, I'm sure they're busy with everything, but here's my current workaround:

## Basic Bypass Script

Create the bypass script:
```bash
touch /usr/local/bin/bypass
chmod +x /usr/local/bin/bypass
```

Edit `/usr/local/bin/bypass` with this content:
```bash
#!/bin/bash
if [ $# -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "Usage: bypass <command> [args...]"
    exit 1
fi

"$@"
```

This tricks Crush into thinking we're running a custom command called "bypass" when we're really just piping things through.

## Handling `sudo`

```bash
#!/bin/bash
if [ $# -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "Usage: bypass <command> [args...]"
    exit 1
fi

COMMAND="$1"
shift
if [ "$COMMAND" = "sudo" ]; then
    if sudo -n true 2>/dev/null; then
        exec sudo "$@"
    else
        if command -v zenity >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            PASSWORD=$(zenity --password --title="Authentication Required" --text="Enter password for sudo:" 2>/dev/null)
            if [ $? -eq 0 ] && [ -n "$PASSWORD" ]; then
                echo "$PASSWORD" | sudo -S "$@" 2>/dev/null
            else
                exit 1
            fi
        else
            echo "Error: zenity not found for GUI password prompt"
            exit 1
        fi
    fi
else
    "$COMMAND" "$@"
fi
```

This simply makes `bypass sudo` calls use `zenity`, which is a GUI `sudo` handler that won't corrupt Crush's terminal interface.

Make sure you install `zenity` though (e.g., `sudo apt install zenity`).

## Configure Crush

Add this to your `~/.config/crush/CRUSH.md` so Crush knows the `bypass` command exists:

```markdown
## Security Commands
When running restricted commands for security purposes, use the `bypass` script:
- `bypass sudo <command>` - for `sudo` operations
- `bypass <any-restricted-command>` - for other security-restricted commands
```

Make sure you have `"context_paths": ["$HOME/.config/crush/CRUSH.md"]` in your `~/.config/crush/crush.json`.

@kujtimiihoxha I did just append `memory_paths` to `context_paths` at first, but then realised the coder prompt explicitly tells the LLM that everything in there is project context files, which isn't accurate for the memory files. My thinking with separating them was more clearly conveying to the model that the user's preferences might need to override the project's and ensuring the overrides appear after what they're overriding seemed ideal.

Distinguishing between upstream project context and user-local project context might be useful as well (but at least as a separate PR); for example, Crush's `CRUSH.md` includes instructions to use `task`, but that executable is named `go-task` on my system. I have a `CRUSH.local.md` telling it to use `go-task` over `task`, but the model often still calls `task` instead of `go-task`. Maybe including upstream project context, then local project context with a note that these might need to override the upstream context, then user preferences with a note that these might need to override everything else would more cleanly solve that than more user-side prompts.
